job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Fatima Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My day starts with a spreadsheet, not a coffee. I do bookkeeping for six stall owners at the Saturday market in Bellmere, and I've built a little workflow where an AI assistant sorts their receipts and I check the output before it goes to them. That brings in about enough for my half of the rent, because I share a room in a flat with my cousin Noor. The rest of the day is applications and a networking call or two. I graduated from Ostrander University in business and finance with a marketing minor, top of the class, and interned at a fintech start-up and at a children's charity's finance team. Four months out, I have 44,000 of debt and no offer, which makes the whole thing feel like a joke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, it's a useful tool and nothing more, and the people predicting a revolution were selling something. I'd tell friends to use it for the boring parts and not worry. Online I'd probably still push for rules on how firms use it, since even a modest tool can be misused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my problem has nothing to do with AI. I have debt, a thin cushion, and there are very few trainee roles within reach of Bellmere. My side work keeps me afloat, but a bookkeeping side hustle isn't a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the six stall owners and try to get to twelve by the end of the year. I'd send applications to finance teams in charities and councils, where my internship counts. I'd also look at a part-time job at one of the firms that hires on short contracts, just to get a reference on my record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, mostly. I'm anxious about money more than anything. I know how to keep busy, but busy doesn't clear 44,000.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would a plateau change your bookkeeping side work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would hardly change, because the tool is what lets me serve six people instead of two. The danger is that the stall owners learn to run it themselves and don't need me. Then I'd have to sell advice instead of data entry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the government if jobs stay scarce?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want debt relief tied to public service and some form of national traineeship. The big firms get tax breaks, so they can fund a year of paid training for each new graduate they decline to hire.

I'd still push for **rules** on how firms use it.
think: My problem has nothing to do with AI: **debt**, a thin cushion and few trainee roles near Bellmere.
A bookkeeping side hustle isn't a **pension**.
do: Grow from six to **twelve** stall owners by the end of the year.
Apply to finance teams at charities and **councils**, where my internship counts.
Take a short-contract role for the **reference**.
feel: **Anxious** about money more than anything, and busy doesn't clear 44,000.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what I've been telling people for a year: learn it now. At work and online I'd share what works, with templates, because most people aren't taught. And I'd say that the gains need sharing, with training funded by the firms that cut staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm in the exposed group even though I'm ahead of it. Entry-level checking and reporting is what the tools do best, so there are fewer jobs for people who do the same. I have an edge in the sense that I can run the tools, but a lot of people with my degree will have it too within a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn my side work into a proper one-person firm, with a name, a contract and a small price rise. I'd add services for small shops that the tools can't do alone, like talking someone through a cash-flow crisis. I'd also pick up a certificate in management accounting, and apply for jobs where AI is part of the description.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and nervous at once. There's more to build, but less certainty that my tools will remain special.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use these tools every day. What would you tell a graduate who doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing stays special for long. If a stall owner can do the receipts on their own phone, I need to sell the thing they can't do themselves, which is telling them what the numbers mean. So I'd go and spend a month learning small business advice from people who do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the stall owners stop needing you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them it takes two weeks of daily use to get good, and that you check everything, because the thing makes up numbers sometimes. I'd tell them to build one small useful thing, and to show it at an interview.

The gains need **sharing**, with training paid for by firms that cut staff.

Study a **management accounting** certificate and apply where AI is in the job description.

steps.text: Set up a one-person bookkeeping firm with contracts and a small price rise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments need to move now, and that includes a payment to every adult from the gains. People would call it radical, but 2028 isn't a long way off. I'd be on social media every day arguing for it and asking firms to publish their plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be scared, I won't pretend otherwise. My side work gets hit the same way as the jobs I'm applying to, so I'm not safer than anyone. I'd probably have eighteen months where my skills are worth something and after that, I'm guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, I'd sit down and list every way I can earn without a thinking-work job, like running errands, helping older people with their phones, even driving for a delivery app. I'd move my savings into something safe. I'd also join the groups pushing for income support and write to my local representative, because the early ones to speak get heard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A rush of adrenaline, then fear. It's the kind of fear where you want to do something immediately, and I'd probably overdo it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What would your first week look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Noor works in a call centre, which goes first. If she loses her job, we can't pay the rent on the flat, so we'd both be back with relatives, which isn't possible for me with my family. That is the scenario I can't plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else would be hit in your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad drives a bus and my mum cleans offices, so the physical jobs last longer, but they can't carry me and my debt. They'd try, though, and that's the part I hate.

say: Governments must move now, including a **payment** to every adult from the gains.
Firms should **publish** their plans for what they'll do.
think: My side work gets hit like the jobs I'm applying for, so I'm **no safer** than anyone.
I'd have maybe **eighteen months** where my skills are worth something.
do: List every way to earn without a thinking-work job, even **delivery** driving.
Move savings somewhere **safe** and write to my local representative.
feel: **Adrenaline** first, then fear, and I'd probably overdo it.
S2.quote: My cousin Noor works in a call centre, which goes first. If she loses her job, we can't pay the rent on the flat
fieldNote: Shared rent means a **household** risk: her cousin's call centre job goes first.
Admits her tool skills give no real **shelter** from AGI.
Reaches for both action and income-support politics, as her outlook predicts.

steps.text: List every non-desk way to earn, including delivery driving
Move my small savings into a safe account
Join an income-support campaign and write to my representative

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do this properly, and we should. Five years is enough for public retraining, an income floor and rules on firms that cut jobs. I'd talk to my friends about it and not just doom-scroll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm a little excited, because five years lets me try one more thing. I could build a small firm that serves other small firms, and it would be established before the big shift. If it works, I'm the person who knows how to bring AI into a small business, and that's useful longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any finance job going to get a salary, and keep the freelancing in the evenings. I'd put 500 a month at the loan, and the rest into the freelance business. By year three I'd be offering a full package to small firms, so even if the big roles shrink, I have my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful but wary. I know five years goes quickly if you stand still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having five years do to your debt plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably clear about a third of the loan and ask for whatever relief is on offer. The risk is that I'm paying while the pay is dropping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you try to stay useful to employers by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay useful by being the person who can explain and check what the tools produce. Employers will still need someone who answers for the numbers, even if the machine produces them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good news and also a reason to get serious. Ten years is enough to retrain a whole country if the government cared, and I'd say so. I'd also say to my friends that complacency is the real risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly safe, to be honest. I can adjust over ten years, and I expect to be doing something that doesn't exist yet. The debt will be mostly paid by then, which feels like the real finish line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a finance role with a firm that trains people, stay two or three years, then go out on my own with a small advisory practice. I'd clear the loan by year seven, put some money into a pension and learn the next generation of tools as they arrive. I'd also teach a night class on AI bookkeeping for market sellers, since I enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit impatient. Ten years is a lot, but I'd want to use every one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you build?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a small advisory firm for small businesses, with AI doing the routine work and me doing the judgement. It's the thing I'm already trying on a tiny scale.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets harder for you if people expect slow change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slow change makes people complacent, and I'd have to keep pushing myself. A friend who stays relaxed for nine years and starts in year ten is in real trouble.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two year one, because I'd have no time for the freelance firm to grow and my cousin Noor's job is the first to go. What would help is an income floor, a pause on the loan and training paid by the firms that cut people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'd like people to stop treating graduates like we're lucky to be here. We have skills, we have a lot of energy and we're ready to learn. We just need the door to open for a few of us.

headlineQuote: I'd like people to stop treating graduates like we're lucky to be here. We have skills, we have a lot of energy and we're ready to learn.
portrait: Fatima is 23, top of her class, shares a room with her cousin Noor and carries **44,000** of debt.
She uses AI tools daily and runs a small bookkeeping side business for six market stall owners.
She is curious and moves early, but knows that her edge is **temporary**.
Progressive on politics, she backs income floors and funded retraining, and gets calmer as the time grows.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario, because her cousin's job goes first and the shared rent would collapse.
whatWouldHelp: An **income floor**, a pause on the loan and training paid for by firms that cut staff.
